t: 3192. Minimum Operations to Make Binary Array Elements Equal to One II
o: Each operation flips a suffix of the binary array; minimize operations to reach all ones. Key observation: process left to right — flipping at index i affects only positions ≥ i, so once position i is fixed to 1 by earlier decisions it never changes again. In example 1 the effective values force a flip whenever the (parity-adjusted) current bit is 0, yielding 4 operations; example 2 needs one flip at index 1.
k: Scan left to right; a suffix flip at i leaves positions < i untouched.
Track flip parity: the effective value of nums[i] is nums[i] XOR flips_so_far.
Whenever the effective value is 0, we must flip here: count it and toggle parity.

a.i: Because each fix at index i is forced (the only way to change position i without disturbing earlier fixed positions is a flip starting exactly at i), the greedy is optimal. One integer parity makes the whole algorithm O(n).
s: For each x: eff = x XOR flip; if eff == 0, increment ans and toggle flip.
a.t: O(n) — single pass with constant work

a.i: Directly simulate: whenever the current element (after applying pending flips naively) is 0, flip the entire suffix. This is O(n²) but validates the greedy and matches the operation definition literally.
s: Scan i from 0; if nums[i] == 0, increment answer and flip all elements from i to end.
a.t: O(n²) — each trigger flips up to n elements

w: Always present the parity-scan solution; the brute force is only for sanity-checking. Pitfall: thinking you may flip anywhere (you can, but any optimal schedule is equivalent to the greedy set of flip points). Related problems: minimum suffix-flip operations on prefixes (LC 3191) uses the mirror-image logic. Follow-up: generalize to making all elements equal to an arbitrary target t — just compare against t instead of 1.
